keyTakeaways: Halloween in the Philippines runs 31 October to 2 November; only 1 and 2 November are non-working days (Proclamation No. 1006 for 2026, No. 1427 for 2027), and 31 October is a working day.
A 1934 account of pangangaluluwa describes 4 to 8 singers posing as souls, a five- or ten-centavo gift, and a real trick: chickens taken and furniture stacked as a mock tomb.
Folklorist Maximo Ramos (1968, 1969) called the aswang a 'congeries of beliefs'; the manananggal splits at the waist, though five regions tell of one that splits at the neck.
Greeting family abroad: 48.3% of shared SubhSandesh pages are opened on a phone, and Manila (UTC+8) is 4 hours ahead of Dubai.

faqs.question: Do Filipinos celebrate Halloween?
faqs.answer: Yes, mostly as costume parties and mall or subdivision trick-or-treat on 31 October. The bigger observance is Undas on 1 and 2 November, when families visit and tend their relatives' graves, so Halloween works as the playful eve before the serious days.

faqs.question: Is Undas a long weekend in 2026?
faqs.answer: Yes. Halloween falls on Saturday 31 October 2026, All Saints' Day on Sunday 1 November, and Proclamation No. 1006 adds Monday 2 November as an additional special non-working day. In 2027 the three days run Sunday to Tuesday under Proclamation No. 1427.

faqs.question: What do Filipinos bring to the cemetery on All Saints' Day?
faqs.answer: Candles, flowers and food, after cleaning and often repainting the tomb. Francisco Demetrio's 1993 study describes families who spruce up the graves of relatives, light candles and bedeck them with flowers, because the dead are believed to keep caring for the living.

faqs.question: On which night was pangangaluluwa sung?
faqs.answer: Toribio de Castro's 1934 account and UP Diliman's dictionary of Filipino music terms both place it on All Souls' Day, 2 November. Many current descriptions say the eve of All Saints' Day instead; practice probably varied by town, and no source we found settles it.

faqs.question: What does 'Magandang gabi po' mean?
faqs.answer: It means 'Good evening', with 'po' marking respect for the person addressed. In the 1934 account, pangangaluluwa singers rang a small bell and then called out this greeting before starting their song.

faqs.question: Did pangangaluluwa singers really play tricks?
faqs.answer: Yes, according to de Castro's 1934 account. While the group sang, two or three members quietly took chickens, papayas, squashes or bananas, and by morning ladders, benches and chairs stood across the street arranged as a mock tomb with candle stubs.

faqs.question: What is the difference between an aswang and a manananggal?
faqs.answer: Aswang is the umbrella term for a family of shape-shifting creatures that folklorist Maximo Ramos called a 'congeries of beliefs'. The manananggal is one type: a woman by day whose upper body detaches at the waist at night and flies off to hunt.

faqs.question: Who was Maximo Ramos?
faqs.answer: A folklorist who spent decades on Philippine lower mythology. He published 'Belief in Ghouls in Contemporary Philippine Society' in Western Folklore in 1968 and The Aswang Complex in Philippine Folklore in 1969, research he said began with a question from his UCLA mentor, Wayland Hand.

faqs.question: What time should I send a Halloween message to the Philippines from Dubai?
faqs.answer: Manila is on UTC+8 with no daylight saving, 4 hours ahead of Dubai and 5 ahead of Riyadh. A message sent at 4 pm in Dubai on 31 October lands at 8 pm in Manila, before families leave for the cemetery the next morning.

faqs.question: Is it rude to send a Halloween joke during Undas?
faqs.answer: On 1 and 2 November it can be, because those days are for remembering the family's dead. Keep jokes and costume pictures to 31 October, and switch to a plain message, a prayer or a call for Undas itself.

article.contentMarkdown:
# Halloween in the Philippines: Undas, Souls' Songs and the Aswang

Halloween in the Philippines runs for three days, not one. Costume parties and mall trick-or-treat take 31 October, then Undas, the family visit to the graves, takes 1 and 2 November, the two days the government makes non-working in both 2026 and 2027. The older Filipino door-knock is *pangangaluluwa* (from *kaluluwa*, "soul"): singers posing as the dead, printed in a 1934 account.

Families split by work abroad usually swap greetings by link that week. Across SubhSandesh, 48.3% of shared pages are opened on a phone and each page averages 11.1 views; both are platform-wide figures, not Halloween data. Below: the 2026 and 2027 calendar, five ways pangangaluluwa differs from trick-or-treating, what the folklorist Maximo Ramos recorded about the *aswang*, and how to greet family abroad without trampling the cemetery days.

## What is Undas, and where does Halloween fit?

Undas is what Filipinos call All Saints' Day and All Souls' Day, 1 and 2 November, the days families go back to their home towns to clean, decorate and sit with their relatives' graves. Halloween on 31 October is the imported, playful eve; Undas is the main event, and it is about the family's own dead rather than monsters.

The Jesuit folklorist Francisco Demetrio described the core of it in a [1993 paper in UST's *Philippiniana Sacra*](https://philsacra.ust.edu.ph/admin/downloadarticle?id=86888D9E93DA27D1C81E253CCBFF187E): people "flock to the cemeteries, spruce up the graves of relatives, light candles and bedeck them with flowers." He traced the devotion to a belief that the dead keep a special interest in living relatives, helping fishers to good catches, farmers to plentiful corn and rice, and children to grow up healthy.

That belief is why the visit is usually a family reunion with food, not a quick stop. Relatives who rarely meet sit together beside the *puntod* (tomb) while the candles burn down.

Demetrio also recorded a planting rite for the two days. The planter buries three strands of human hair, nine small hot peppers and nine *tapok-tapok* seashells in exactly three holes, reciting the Hail Mary while digging.

## The calendar: 31 October to 2 November in 2026 and 2027

The days off are 1 and 2 November; 31 October stays a working day in both years. [Proclamation No. 1006](https://lawphil.net/executive/proc/proc2025/proc_1006_2025.html) sets the 2026 dates and [Proclamation No. 1427](https://lawphil.net/executive/proc/proc2026/proc_1427_2026.html), dated 8 September 2026, the 2027 ones. The table below sets the three days side by side.

| Date | 2026 | 2027 | What happens |
|---|---|---|---|
| 31 Oct, Halloween | Saturday, working day | Sunday, working day | Costume parties, mall and subdivision trick-or-treat |
| 1 Nov, All Saints' Day | Sunday, special non-working | Monday, special non-working | Main cemetery day; graves cleaned, candles lit |
| 2 Nov, All Souls' Day | Monday, additional special non-working | Tuesday, non-working in the preamble, though the 2027 list prints "special (working)" | Visits continue; the 1934 night for pangangaluluwa |

In 2026 the three days run Saturday to Monday, which makes the trip home a long weekend. In 2027 they run Sunday to Tuesday, so check the final word on 2 November before booking a Tuesday-night bus.

Modern Halloween fits into the 31 October slot. Malls run costume parades and store-to-store candy routes, and gated subdivisions set a window for children to go house to house; on the next morning the same families are packing for the province.

## Pangangaluluwa vs trick-or-treating: 5 differences

Pangangaluluwa is a Tagalog custom in which a small group goes from house to house at night, singing as the souls of the dead and asking for alms. The fullest early account we found is Toribio de Castro's, printed in *Philippine Magazine* in November 1934 and reprinted in the journal [*Folklore Studies* in 1958](https://asianethnology.org/article/148016-the-weird-tale-of-the-twelve-hunchbacks-atagalog-folktale.pdf). Each item compares the 1934 custom with trick-or-treat as Filipino children now do it, in the same order: the old way, the new way, the gap.

### 1. Who comes to the door

In 1934 it was a group of four to eight people, playing the souls of the dead, who sang from early evening until dawn. Today it is costumed children with a parent, usually done within a couple of hours. The singers were the dead; the children only dress as monsters.

### 2. What is said at the door

De Castro's group rang a little bell, called "Magandang gabi po" ("Good evening", with *po* for respect) and then sang to a guitar or violin. [UP Diliman's dictionary of Filipino music terms](https://iskomunidad.upd.edu.ph/index.php/MUSDIKS:pangangaluluwa), citing Marialita Yraola in a 1977 *Musika Jornal*, lists four stages: a *Pa-hesus* opening, reminders of good deeds, verses on the Virgin Mary, saints or village life, then the alms and thanks. Trick-or-treat needs three words.

### 3. What the household gives

The 1934 householder "knows his obligation well" and handed over a five- or ten-centavo coin. The UP entry calls the gift alms or donations, and gives *palimos* (begging for alms) as another name for the custom. Trick-or-treaters get wrapped sweets.

### 4. Where the takings go

The 1934 singers paid for candles and a morning Mass the next day before splitting what was left. The reasoning was devotional: souls guilty of venial sins were believed to wander, begging alms for candles to pray their way into Purgatory. Trick-or-treat candy is simply kept.

### 5. The trick

This is the surprise in the 1934 text: pangangaluluwa had a real trick. While the singing went on, two or three others quietly took chickens, papayas, squashes or bananas. Next morning, ladders, benches and chairs turned up across the street arranged as a tomb, with candle stubs and chicken feathers beside it, and householders blamed "the hungry wandering souls."

One date problem is worth knowing. De Castro and the UP entry both place pangangaluluwa on All Souls' Day, 2 November, while many current descriptions put it on the eve of All Saints'. We found no source that settles which towns used which night.

## Aswang and manananggal: what Maximo Ramos recorded

The Philippines brings its own monsters to Halloween, and the folklorist Maximo Ramos spent decades cataloguing them. He published "Belief in Ghouls in Contemporary Philippine Society" in *Western Folklore* in 1968 and *The Aswang Complex in Philippine Folklore* in 1969, reprinted by Phoenix in 1990.

Film scholar Bliss Cua Lim summarises his work in a [2015 *Kritika Kultura* article from Ateneo de Manila](https://hdl.handle.net/1807/141534). Ramos called the aswang complex a "congeries of beliefs" and sorted it into types echoing Europe's vampires, witches, ghouls and werewolves, while admitting they "do not fit exactly." His were-beast is usually a weredog or a werepig, not a wolf.

His manananggal is "an attractive woman by day, buxom, long-haired, and light complexioned" who, at night, "discards [her] lower body from the waist down and flies." Lim lists regional names: *wuwug* in Boholano, *magcucutud* in Pampangueño and *anananggal* in Bicol. Accounts from Aklan, Siquijor, Cebu, Bicol and Bohol describe a rarer kind that splits at the neck instead.

An aswang is usually heard before it is seen. Lim notes the bird cries *tiktik* and *kikik*, and wings flapping on the roof, *wakwak* or *kaskas*.

Ramos added a warning that still applies: printing an oral story gives it a tidiness living legend lacks. Lim adds that Ramos credited a single question from his UCLA mentor, Wayland Hand, "What's an aswang?", with starting decades of research.

## Greeting family abroad over Halloween and Undas

For a Filipino working abroad, 31 October can be silly and 1–2 November should be about the family's dead. Manila is UTC+8 with no daylight saving, so an 8 pm Manila message lands at 4 pm in Dubai (UTC+4) and 3 pm in Riyadh (UTC+3). Original lines to send, Tagalog first with an English gloss:

- "Happy Halloween, anak! Walang aswang dito, pero may kakaning naghihintay sa'yo." ("Happy Halloween, child! No aswang here, but there's rice cake waiting for you.")
- "Kahit nasa kabilang dagat ka, ikaw pa rin ang paborito kong kalabasa." ("Even across the sea, you're still my favourite pumpkin.")
- "Sinindihan ko na ang kandila para kay Lolo. Ikaw naman, buksan mo ang video call mamaya." ("I've lit the candle for Grandpa. Your turn: open the video call later.")
- "Nasa sementeryo kami, katabi ni Lola. May puwesto ka pa rin sa tabi namin." ("We're at the cemetery beside Lola. There's still a place for you beside us.")

Send the first two on 31 October and keep the last two for Undas. For the playful night, the [interactive Halloween card with up to six photos](https://subhsandesh.in/happy-halloween) takes about 5 minutes; in family mode its closing question becomes "Will you be my favourite little pumpkin?", and you get an email the first time they answer. Its interface is English, but the letter and names can be typed in Tagalog.

For a parent or sibling who will reread it on a break, the [premium Halloween page with a 60-second voice note](https://subhsandesh.in/happy-halloween-premium) takes about 10 minutes. It holds up to 12 photos, can stay locked until a time you set, and carries one reply of up to 280 characters back to your inbox. Family photos are private, and 38.5% of SubhSandesh creators add a password before sharing.

When the person abroad is a partner and the real message is that you miss them, the [miss-you page built for couples apart](https://subhsandesh.in/missyou-gf) is the better fit than a pumpkin. It was built for distance, with a countdown to a reunion date and "open when" letters.

## When to skip the Halloween card during Undas

Skip it on 1 and 2 November for a family in mourning. Demetrio's point stands: the visit is a devotion to relatives who are believed to still care, and a cartoon ghost reads as a joke at the graveside.

Skip it for a grandparent who is not comfortable in English, because every button is in English. Skip it for a barangay party too: each page greets a single person and cannot invite a whole street. And if you will be at the puntod yourself, light the candle in person; 90.9% of started SubhSandesh pages get published, and none of them replaces turning up.

structuralLimitations: No Halloween usage data exists in facts.md; the four first-party figures are platform-wide and labelled as such in the body.

Prompt said the 2027 proclamation 'may not be out'. False: Proclamation No. 1427 (8 Sep 2026) sets 2027. Its preamble declares 2 Nov 2027 an additional special (non-working) day, but its Section 1 list prints All Souls' Day under 'C. Special (Working) Day'; the post states both. officialgazette.gov.ph and pco.gov.ph returned 403 (bot wall, not worked around), so the Lawphil copies were read.

Common online claim that pangangaluluwa is sung on the eve of All Saints' Day is not what the two sources read say: de Castro (1934/1958) and UP MUSDIKS (citing Yraola 1977) both place it on All Souls' Day. The post says practice may have varied and no source settles it.

Maximo Ramos's own works (Western Folklore 1968, doi 10.2307/1498104; 1969, doi 10.2307/1499218; The Aswang Complex, 1969/1990) are on JSTOR or in print and were not read; every Ramos claim comes via Lim 2015, which quotes him with page numbers. Titles and years verified via Crossref and Lim's bibliography.

Mall and subdivision trick-or-treat is described from general knowledge without a non-competitor source: the PTV News feature b4 used was unreachable on 2026-10-14 and Philippine Studies (philippinestudies.net) and journals.ateneo.edu did not resolve from this machine. No number is attached to the claim.
